insights.concise_text: The proposed methodology addresses the extremely large action space by using Go-Explore to extract high reward trajectories and then training a Seq2Seq model on them.

triple.subject: the proposed methodology
triple.object: the extremely large action space

insights.concise_text: Go-Explore is suitable for the paper's experiments because it explores sparse-reward environments sample efficiently and the experiments focus on final policy performance.

triple.subject: Go-Explore
triple.object: focus on final performance of our policy

insights.concise_text: Phase 2 trains a Seq2Seq model on trajectories found in phase 1, where those trajectories consist of observation, action, and reward tuples.

triple.subject: Phase 2
triple.object: trajectories found in phase 1

insights.concise_text: The Seq2Seq policy maps observations to actions by encoding observation tokens and decoding action tokens, matching the POMDP definitions of observations and actions as token sequences.

triple.subject: the Seq2Seq policy
triple.object: observations and actions as token sequences

insights.concise_text: CoinCollector's +1 reward only after collecting the coin and its need for at least 30 actions on hard games make it suitable for testing exploration capabilities.

triple.subject: CoinCollector
triple.object: suitability for testing exploration capabilities

insights.concise_text: CookingWorld is used to evaluate generalization because CoinCollector has a very limited action space while CookingWorld has 4,440 games with 222 different levels of difficulty.

triple.subject: CookingWorld
triple.object: generalization capabilities of our proposed approach

insights.concise_text: The Zero-Shot setting tests the stronger generalization claimed for training a Seq2Seq model on Go-Explore trajectories by evaluating on unseen test games.

triple.subject: Zero-Shot
triple.object: unseen test games

insights.concise_text: The paper's more challenging environments contrast with standard benchmarks by requiring multiple words at each step, while standard benchmarks require no more than two words.

triple.subject: more challenging environments
triple.object: standard benchmarks requiring no more than two words

insights.concise_text: The episodic discovery bonus is limited to very small action and state spaces, so CoinCollector's five admissible commands make it a compatible exploration baseline.

triple.subject: the episodic discovery bonus
triple.object: games with very small action and state spaces

insights.concise_text: DRRN corresponds to the second reinforcement learning approach because it learns one Q-function that scores admissible actions rather than generating actions token by token.

triple.subject: DRRN
triple.object: one $Q$-function that scores all possible actions

insights.concise_text: Phase 1 of Go-Explore extracts high-performing trajectories that train a simple Seq2Seq model, which achieves the highest score among all methods in the single CookingWorld setting.

triple.subject: phase 1 of Go-Explore trajectories
triple.object: Seq2Seq model score among all methods in single CookingWorld

insights.concise_text: The Seq2Seq model trained on phase 1 of Go-Explore trajectories achieves the highest score among all methods but scores 9.4% lower than phase 1 of Go-Explore.

triple.subject: Seq2Seq model trained on phase 1 of Go-Explore trajectories
triple.object: total score to 9.4% lower than phase 1 of Go-Explore

insights.concise_text: In CoinCollector hard games where level 30 indicates the shortest path, phase 1 of Go-Explore finds an always optimal 30-step trajectory.

triple.subject: phase 1 of Go-Explore
triple.object: CoinCollector hard games with level 30 shortest path

insights.concise_text: The joint CookingWorld setting trains a single model on all games at once, and all evaluated models achieved lower performance than in the single game setting.

triple.subject: joint CookingWorld setting
triple.object: lower performance compared to the single game setting for all evaluated models

insights.concise_text: The state representation limitation is especially visible in joint CookingWorld, where 222 games are repeated 20 times with different entities and room maps.

triple.subject: joint CookingWorld repeated games
triple.object: state representation limitation through overlapping descriptions

insights.concise_text: The hardest CookingWorld games require a very long sequence of actions, and most lost games for Go-Explore Seq2Seq are in the hardest set.

triple.subject: very long action sequences in hardest CookingWorld games
triple.object: Go-Explore Seq2Seq zero-shot performance

item.text: Counting restoration actions lets Go-Explore be compared one-to-one with count-based reward algorithms, and phase 1 of Go-Explore uses approximately half the interactions to find an optimal trajectory
triple: one-to-one exploration-efficiency comparison showing phase 1 of Go-Explore uses approximately half the interactions

item.text: Go-Explore uses given admissible actions during random exploration, but Zork I and Z-Machine games do not provide them, so Go-Explore would have a hard time finding good trajectories.
triple: absence of admissible actions in Zork I and Z-Machine games

item.text: The zero-shot split stratifies recipes 1, 2 and 3 equally, and Go-Explore Seq2Seq solves almost half of the unseen games.
triple: stratified zero-shot split by recipes 1, 2 and 3
Go-Explore Seq2Seq solving almost half of the unseen games

item.text: The hand-tailored CookingWorld solution obtained up to 91.9% of the maximum possible score across 514 test games but relies on entity extraction and template filling, which limits generalization.
triple: generalization of the hand-tailored CookingWorld solution despite 91.9% of maximum possible score
